slides.text: After a viral fever damaged my olfactory nerve, the world turned into a photograph behind glass—I could see the ocean and the bakery down the street, but I couldn't smell salt or warm bread anymore. Worse, I was terrified I was forgetting the scent of my wife, Maeve, who had been working as a botanical perfumer in Grasse when we first fell in love.

Every evening for a year, Maeve locked herself in her attic laboratory surrounded by three hundred amber essential-oil bottles, testing molecular compounds on paper strips and holding them under my nose. 'Anything?' she would ask softly. Night after night, I had to shake my head, watching the quiet heartbreak in her eyes as another formula failed to cross the damaged wiring in my brain.

On our fifth anniversary, I woke up to find a single drop of clear oil dabbed onto my pillowcase. I breathed in—and suddenly, through ten months of grey static, a faint, electric chord broke through: wet cedarwood, crushed mint, and the cheap vanilla soap from the hostel in Provence where we sheltered from a thunderstorm at twenty-two. I opened my eyes to find Maeve crying against my chest. 'You came back to me,' I whispered.
